fields.foundation: The Aksumite Empire arose in the highlands of northern Ethiopia and Eritrea around the first century CE, though its roots go back to the pre-Aksumite civilisation that had absorbed South Arabian cultural and linguistic influences centuries earlier. The earliest historical reference to Aksum as a functioning polity appears in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a Greek merchant's guide of the mid-first century CE. It names the metropolis of the Axomites and describes the local ruler Zoskales as versed in Greek letters, early evidence of the region's engagement with the Graeco-Roman world. The guide describes the port of Adulis on the Red Sea coast as a major hub for the export of ivory, tortoiseshell, rhinoceros horn and other African goods, which suggests that Aksum was already overtaking the declining Kingdom of Kush as a leading supplier of African luxury goods to Roman markets. Aksum lay between the Ethiopian highland agricultural zone and the Red Sea coast, and so controlled the movement of goods between the African interior and the maritime routes linking Rome, Arabia and India. King Endubis introduced Aksumite coinage around 270 CE, making Aksum one of the very few states of the ancient world to issue its own gold coins. Gold, silver and bronze issues, inscribed mainly in Greek and later also in Ge'ez, enabled Aksum to participate fully in the Mediterranean monetary economy. In the third century the Persian prophet Mani reportedly counted Aksum alongside Rome, Persia and China as one of the four great kingdoms of the world.
fields.socioeconomy: The Aksumite economy was commercial, built on Aksum's position as the entrepôt linking the African interior to the Indian Ocean trade network. The port of Adulis handled luxury commodities in volume: ivory from the interior, gold from the lands to the south and west, tortoiseshell from the Red Sea coast, aromatics from the Horn, obsidian and live animals, destined for Roman, Arabian and Indian markets. In return, Aksum imported textiles, glassware, wine, olive oil and metalwork from the Mediterranean world, and spices, cotton and gems from India. Aksumite coins have been found as far afield as southern Arabia and India, which shows that the empire traded across continents. The highlands provided a productive farming base that supported significant urban populations, with terracing, irrigation, ox-drawn ploughs and the cultivation of crops such as teff, wheat and barley. Aksumite society comprised a royal elite, a clergy that gained greatly in prestige and power after the adoption of Christianity under King Ezana in the fourth century, a merchant community of mixed origins, and a large agricultural population. The loss of influence in Yemen to the Sasanian Persians in the 570s cut Aksum off from the eastern shore of the Red Sea and from the revenues of the trans-Arabian trade. The rise of Islam and the Arab conquests of Arabia and Egypt in the seventh century completed Aksum's commercial isolation and ended the trade-based prosperity that had sustained the kingdom for some five centuries.
fields.military: Aksumite military power served the empire's commercial rather than purely territorial ambitions, though at its height it could send forces across the Red Sea and deep into the African interior. The kings led a royal army supplemented by contingents drawn from tributary peoples, and war elephants appear in accounts of Aksumite campaigns and diplomacy. King Ezana's conquest of the Kingdom of Kush around 350 CE reached the Nile and destroyed the remnants of Meroitic power. It removed the last significant rival for control of African trade routes to Egypt and was the most consequential military achievement of the empire's classical phase. Ezana's inscriptions, including the trilingual Ezana Stone in Ge'ez, Sabaean and Greek, record campaigns against peoples across what is now Sudan, Eritrea and the Ethiopian interior, and present the king as a divinely sanctioned conqueror who destroyed towns and deported populations. Aksumite reach was greatest in the Yemen campaigns of King Kaleb (r. c. 514–542 CE). Around 525 a major seaborne expedition, undertaken with the encouragement of the Byzantine Emperor Justin I, overthrew the Himyarite king Dhu Nuwas, who had persecuted the Christians of Najran, and installed a Christian client ruler in South Arabia. Historians such as Stuart Munro-Hay have described this venture as Aksum's swan song as a great power, since it overextended the empire's military and financial resources: within a few years the Aksumite general Abraha had made himself effectively independent ruler of Yemen. The Sasanian conquest of Yemen in the 570s showed the limits of a military system that had never developed the logistical depth needed to sustain power across the Red Sea against a determined imperial opponent.
fields.governance: The Aksumite system combined central royal authority with a hierarchy of subordinate kings and local chiefs and, from the fourth century, an increasingly powerful Christian church. The Aksumite ruler bore the title negusa nagast, king of kings: tributary rulers acknowledged Aksumite suzerainty while retaining local authority. The coinage carried the king's image and titles across the trading world in Greek and Ge'ez. The monumental stelae of Aksum itself, carved granite monoliths often called obelisks, marked the tombs of the Aksumite elite and expressed royal power. The largest measured some 33 metres, though it probably fell during or soon after its erection. The adoption of Christianity under Ezana in the mid-fourth century, following the influence of his Syrian-Greek tutor Frumentius, who was consecrated as the first Bishop of Aksum by Athanasius of Alexandria, made the church a main support of government. Frumentius, remembered in Ethiopia as Abba Salama, oversaw the integration of Christian religious authority into the existing royal order, and the tie to the patriarchate of Alexandria, which appointed Ethiopia's bishops for some sixteen centuries, began here. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church, which traces its institutional lineage directly to this conversion, outlasted the Aksumite dynasty by more than a millennium. The empire governed through direct royal control over the highland core and tributary arrangements with peripheral peoples, a system adequate during the commercial boom but fragile once the trade revenues sustaining the centre contracted.
fields.impact: The Aksumite Empire's influence was commercial, religious, cultural and architectural, and it extended far beyond the boundaries of the state itself. As one of the great powers of late antiquity, Aksum was a principal conduit for African goods entering the Graeco-Roman and Indian Ocean economies. Ezana's conversion made Aksum one of the first states to adopt Christianity officially and the first to place the cross on its coinage, decades before Christianity became the official religion of the Roman Empire under Theodosius I. The Ethiopian Orthodox tradition that began with it is one of the oldest continuous Christian institutions in the world. Ge'ez, the language of Aksumite inscriptions, became the liturgical and literary language of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, and its script, which the Aksumites developed into a fully vocalised alphabet, is still used to write Amharic, Tigrinya and other languages today. The great stelae of Aksum, among the most ambitious monuments in ancient Africa, required technical skill and organisation, and they shaped later Ethiopian building traditions. The Zagwe dynasty, which succeeded Aksum, built the famous rock-hewn churches of Lalibela in a style showing clear Aksumite architectural influence, so Aksum's culture survived its political collapse. The Ethiopian royal tradition of descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, codified in the fourteenth-century Kebra Nagast and traced through the kings of Aksum, shaped Ethiopian identity, statecraft and diplomacy for centuries after the empire's fall.
fields.decline: The Aksumite Empire declined under a series of shocks that destroyed the trade on which its prosperity rested. The first came with the Sasanian conquest of Yemen in the 570s. A Sasanian expeditionary force under the general Wahrez took Sana'a, overthrew the Abyssinian rulers of Yemen, the successors of Abraha, and installed Persian rule, which cut Aksum off from the eastern shore of the Red Sea and ended decades of commercial and strategic influence over the Arabian trade. The second and more damaging blow was the rise of Islam. The Arab conquests of Arabia, the Levant and Egypt in the seventh century transferred control of the Red Sea trade to Muslim powers whose networks increasingly bypassed Aksum, even though relations between the two were at first cordial, Aksum having sheltered early Muslim emigrants around 615. Aksumite coinage, issued for over three centuries, ceased around the early seventh century, a strong indication that the commercial economy was in decline. A third pressure was probably environmental: deprived of trade revenues, the highland farmland around the capital appears to have been worked ever harder, and many scholars link the kingdom's contraction to soil erosion, deforestation and declining agricultural productivity. Economic isolation, agricultural degradation and a shrinking population together reduced Aksum from an international commercial power to a regional highland kingdom within two centuries. The political centre shifted southwards, to a capital known in Arabic sources as Kubar, by the ninth century. According to Ethiopian tradition, the last Aksumite king, Dil Na'od, was overthrown by Mara Takla Haymanot, who founded the Zagwe dynasty, though the date of this transition is uncertain and usually placed in the tenth to twelfth century. It ended a dynasty that had ruled for many centuries.
fields.summary: The Aksumite Empire adopted Christianity in the Ethiopian highlands, developed the Ge'ez script and brought north-east Africa into the commercial networks of the ancient world. The religious and written traditions it founded have continued without interruption to the present day.
fields.teaser: One of antiquity's great trading powers, Aksum controlled the Red Sea trade routes and was among the first states to adopt Christianity. Several of its towering granite stelae, often called obelisks, still stand today.
fields.t0: Aksum, in highland Ethiopia and Eritrea, grew rich trading African ivory and gold through its Red Sea port of Adulis.
fields.t1: Under King Ezana it became one of the first states to adopt Christianity, founding Ethiopia's Orthodox tradition.
fields.t2: Cut off from Red Sea trade by Persia and the early Islamic conquests, it shrank into a regional highland kingdom.
fields.dyk: Aksum was one of the very few ancient states to mint its own gold coins, and the first to place the Christian cross on its coinage.
